title: FRM Quant, Lesson 5: Maximum likelihood estimation and the method of moments
subtitle: Two ways to pick the parameters of a distribution, and why that choice decides the final risk number
whyItMatters: Every risk model has to fit a distribution to data, and that fitting always goes through some parameter estimation method. The two common methods give different answers, especially in the tail - which is where the risk number is decided.
openingQuestion: What is the principle behind maximum likelihood estimation?
openingOptions: Pick the parameters that make the observed data most probable
Pick the parameters that minimise the squared error between forecast and outcome
Pick the parameters equal to the plain average of the observations in the sample
Pick the parameters that a panel of industry experts has agreed to propose
explanation: Maximum likelihood inverts the familiar question: instead of asking whether the data fits the parameters, it asks which set of parameters makes the observed data least surprising. Technically we maximise the likelihood function, usually through its logarithm because that is easier to work with. The method of moments is simpler - match the sample moments to the theoretical ones - but statistically less efficient, so it is often used as the starting point for an optimisation algorithm.

diagram.label: Choose a distribution family that suits the nature of the data

Find the parameters that maximise it
Test goodness of fit, especially in the tail

realWorldExample.company: Why the choice of estimation method feeds through to capital
realWorldExample.description: In an operational risk model, the same loss data set can be fitted by the method of moments or by MLE, and the two produce noticeably different tail parameters. Because capital is computed at a very high quantile, a small difference in the tail parameter is magnified into a large difference in the capital number. This is one of the reasons the Basel Committee concluded that internal models for operational risk lacked comparability across banks.

quiz.question: How does the method of moments estimate parameters?
options: Set the theoretical moments equal to the sample moments and solve
Pick the parameters that maximise the probability of the observed data set
Average the parameter estimates taken from several different subsamples
Use last period's parameter values as the estimate for the current period
quiz.explanation: The idea is very direct: if the distribution's mean and variance are functions of the parameters, set them equal to the sample mean and sample variance and solve the system. Simple and always computable, but usually less statistically efficient than MLE. The second option describes maximum likelihood, the third is a resampling scheme rather than an estimator, and the fourth is not estimation at all but a persistence assumption.

quiz.question: Why is estimating a tail parameter particularly hard and sensitive?
options: Because a theoretical distribution has no parameter for its tail
Because very few observations land in the tail
Because supervisors require tail data to be cut from the sample
Because the tail has no bearing on the final risk number
quiz.explanation: This is the central paradox of risk measurement: the most important part of the distribution is the part with the least data. Adding or removing a single extreme observation can shift the estimate substantially, which makes the result unstable through time. Distributions certainly do carry tail parameters, nobody requires extreme data to be excluded, and the tail is precisely what determines the risk number.

quiz.question: After estimating the parameters, what matters most in the goodness-of-fit step for a risk application?
options: The number of parameters, on the basis that more is more reliable
The fit in the centre, where the observations are concentrated
The fit measured separately in the tail of the distribution
The running time of the estimation algorithm on the sample
quiz.explanation: Common goodness-of-fit tests are dominated by the body, where most of the observations sit. A model that passes an overall test can still badly understate the probability in the tail - exactly the region where VaR and Expected Shortfall are computed. More parameters usually mean more overfitting rather than more reliability, and computational cost has nothing to do with whether the fit is trustworthy.

quiz.question: Why is parameter estimation in the tail particularly sensitive?
options: Because tail parameters cannot be estimated by maximum likelihood at all
Because the likelihood function loses its unique solution once extreme values appear
Because the distribution in the tail must always be assumed to be normal
Because so few observations lie there that adding or dropping one moves the result
quiz.explanation: The entire part that determines the capital level sits in the region with the fewest observations - that is the central paradox of risk measurement. One newly arrived extreme event can shift the parameter substantially, and that is not a defect of the method but the nature of the data. Maximum likelihood works perfectly well on tail parameters, extreme values do not destroy uniqueness of the solution, and assuming normality in the tail is exactly the mistake this topic warns against.

quiz.question: By what criterion does maximum likelihood pick a parameter set?
options: The set that makes the data actually observed the most probable
The set that minimises squared error between model and data
The set making the theoretical moments equal the sample ones
The set lying inside the 95% interval of every parameter tried
quiz.explanation: MLE inverts the question: instead of asking what the data says about the parameters, it asks which parameter set makes this exact sequence of numbers least surprising. The third option describes the method of moments - a different route, a different answer, and one that usually diverges most in the tail. Squared error minimisation is least squares, and a confidence interval is an output of estimation rather than a rule for choosing.

practicePrompt.question: You fit a distribution to a loss series using MLE. The overall goodness-of-fit test comes back very strong. For a risk measurement application, what else should be checked?
options: The fit measured separately in the tail, where most of the data is absent
Whether the optimiser ran enough iterations to have converged
Whether the likelihood value beats the method of moments
Whether the sample exceeds the customary thirty observations
practicePrompt.explanation: An overall goodness-of-fit test weights by the number of observations, and the observations sit almost entirely in the body. So a distribution that describes the body very well and the tail very badly still clears an overall test easily - the tail simply has too few points to move the statistic. For a risk application that is the whole problem: VaR and Expected Shortfall read the tail and nothing else, and an error there shows up in no aggregate number at all. You therefore have to inspect the tail on its own, usually with a quantile plot or by comparing realised exceedances against the count the model predicted.

keyTakeaways: MLE picks the parameters that make the observed data most likely to have occurred
The method of moments sets theoretical moments equal to sample moments and solves for the parameters
Tail parameter estimates are highly sensitive because data in that region is extremely sparse
Goodness-of-fit testing has to look at the tail separately, not only at the whole

summary.keyIdea: Choosing an estimation method is a modelling decision with a direct consequence for the risk number, not a neutral technical detail
summary.commonMistake: Accepting a model because it passes an overall goodness-of-fit test, when that test is dominated by the body
summary.action: After fitting a distribution, always plot the tail on its own and compare it against the realised observations

application.title: Try it on real data
application.message: Take a series of daily index returns, compute the mean and standard deviation, then compare the number of days falling more than three standard deviations under the normal distribution with the number that actually occurred.
application.secondary: The gap between those two figures is the most direct visual evidence there is for fat tails.

sections.text: Choosing a distribution family is the first big decision; choosing how to estimate that distribution's parameters is the second, and it gets far less attention despite mattering just as much.

The idea is to invert the usual question. Instead of asking what the data would look like given these parameters, we ask which parameters make the data we already observed least surprising. Technically, we write the likelihood function for the whole sample and find its maximum, usually through the logarithm because sums are easier to handle than products.

left.label: Maximum likelihood
left.text: Statistically more efficient when the sample is large and the distribution family is correctly chosen. The price is that it usually needs a numerical solution and is sensitive to picking the wrong family.

right.label: Method of moments
right.text: Simple, and always computable in closed form. The price is lower efficiency and the possibility of producing parameters outside the valid range on a small sample.

sections.text: The problem lives in the tail

The central paradox of risk measurement: the region that decides the final number is the region with the least data. With only a handful of extreme observations, adding or removing one point can shift the tail parameter substantially, and because capital is computed at a very high quantile, a small parameter difference is magnified into a large difference in the result.

sections.label: Goodness-of-fit tests give false comfort easily
sections.text: The common tests weight by the density of observations, so they mostly reflect the body. A model with an excellent test result can still understate tail probabilities by several orders of magnitude - and that is exactly where the risk lives.

lines: Parameter estimation is not a neutral technical step; it is a modelling decision.
Next lesson: when there is no closed-form solution, we simulate.
